article_title: Towards Data-Informed Teaching Practice: A Model for Integrating Analytics with Teacher Inquiry
citation: Saar, M., Rodríguez-Triana, M. J., & Prieto, L. P. (2022). Towards Data-Informed Teaching Practice: A Model for Integrating Analytics with Teacher Inquiry. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 88–103. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7505
title: Design TLA models to start with purpose rather than problems, keep the inquiry question central, and complement student data with teaching data
description: The article derives design principles for analytics-informed teacher inquiry models from its three DBR iterations. A TLA model "should not focus on problems but should inform teaching practice in general", should "draw attention to an inquiry question", should indicate "how student data could be complemented by teaching data", and should help teachers "divide their teaching analysis into different but logically linked steps". These principles respond to teachers' difficulties with interpretation steps and their tendency to pose questions only about students.
requirements: Models should provide explanations, examples, and prompts for data variety to assist teachers at each step
constraints: The authors note more assistance should be provided to teachers in formulating inquiry questions, as teachers do not always start analysis with them
target_learners: Novice and experienced primary and secondary school teachers
target_learning_goals: Conducting analytics-informed inquiry into teaching practice
examples: The AMTI starts with "purpose" rather than "problem identification" and was reshaped into a circular diagram to emphasize iterative inquiry
key_sources: Saar, M., Rodríguez-Triana, M. J., & Prieto, L. P. (2022). Towards Data-Informed Teaching Practice: A Model for Integrating Analytics with Teacher Inquiry. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 88–103. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7505

article_title: CRITICS - Critical Science Without Borders: Language Models to Promote Critical Thinking in Science Education
citation: Agerri, R., Aldabe, I., Cabrio, E., Cieliebak, M., Deriu, J., Flores, M., Kapočiūtė-Dzikienė, J., Kuizinienė, D., Rico, A., Ruiz-González, A., Soroa, A., Vaškevičius, M. and Villata, S. (2026). CRITICS - Critical Science Without Borders: Language Models to Promote Critical Thinking in Science Education. SEPLN 2026. https://www.hitz.eus/critics
title: Teaching and Learning Sequence (TLS) generator transforming translated scientific literature into structured educational resources
description: The second CRITICS component is a Teaching and Learning Sequence generator that investigates how to transform translated scientific literature into structured educational resources. It works "by analyzing the corpus to identify key concepts and pedagogical approaches, extracting argumentation graphs to generate TLSs". The TLSs specify driving problems/questions, learning objectives focused on competency acquisition, scientific practices including argumentation and critical thinking, and activities for science students, following Design-Based Research and curriculum-aligned teaching-learning.
requirements: argumentation graphs extracted from the corpus
alignment with learning objectives and competency acquisition
constraints: TLSs are developed for topic-specific competency-based assessments in natural sciences and AI
examples: The project cites prior work on teaching-learning sequences in initial teacher training about sound as the science education research tradition it follows.

article_title: Effects of Multimedia-Based Graphic Novel Presentation on Critical Thinking among Students of Different Learning Approaches
citation: Hii, S. C., & Fong, S. F. (2013). Effects of Multimedia-Based Graphic Novel Presentation on Critical Thinking among Students of Different Learning Approaches. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1080061
title: Mandell and Malone's Thinking Like a Historian (TLH) model as a framework for historical thinking in multimedia graphic novel learning
description: The Thinking Like a Historian (TLH) model by Mandell and Malone (2007) serves as a framework and historical literacy method in history teaching and learning. It identifies historical study as a three-step process: asking questions about the past, gathering sources and evaluating evidence, and drawing conclusions supported by evidence. The model organizes investigations through five categories of inquiry questions (Cause and Effect, Change and Continuity, Turning Points, Using the Past, Through Their Eyes) that engage students in historical meaning-making. In this study, the TLH model was incorporated into the design of a multimedia-based graphic novel learning environment to promote critical thinking skills in history learning rather than rote learning, embedding thought-provoking questions within the courseware.
requirements: Requires a constructivist learning environment with questioning approach to motivate learners to expand and find more about the subject area
constraints: The model was applied specifically to history learning about the Japanese Occupation of Malaya 1942-1945 with Malaysian secondary students
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking skills in history learning
Historical thinking skills including developing arguments from evidence
examples: The multimedia learning material 'Japanese Occupation of Malaya 1942-1945' embedded TLH inquiry questions to guide students through the three-step historical process
key_sources: Hii, S. C., & Fong, S. F. (2013). Effects of Multimedia-Based Graphic Novel Presentation on Critical Thinking among Students of Different Learning Approaches. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1018032

article_title: Brief, embedded, spontaneous metacognitive talk indicates thinking like a physicist
citation: Eleanor C. Sayre, Paul W. Irving. (2021). Brief, embedded, spontaneous metacognitive talk indicates thinking like a physicist. https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.7590
title: Schematization of thinking like a physicist as five epistemological dimensions drawn from beliefs inventories
description: The article schematizes thinking like a physicist (TLP) by reinterpreting the CLASS and MPEX beliefs inventories, treating their expert-validated statements as a 'basis set' for what TLP means in undergraduate coursework. The five dimensions are physics in the real world, connections among physics, sense making, problem solving, and effort and aptitude. Physicists 'emphatically do not endorse a fixed mindset, rote formula or procedure use, or compartmentalization of physics classroom material.' These dimensions are not wholly distinct, and individual survey items can test several at once.
requirements: The dimensions are drawn from expert-validated instruments, the CLASS and MPEX, whose statements represent curated lists of what it means to think like a physicist in an undergraduate classroom context.
constraints: The authors note the dimensions 'are not wholly distinct, and individual items on the CLASS test several of them at once.'
target_learning_goals: developing physicist-like epistemological beliefs and commitments
examples: The sense-making dimension is described as physicists' belief that it is important to make sense of physical scenarios, as opposed to blindly applying formulas and procedures
key_sources: Eleanor C. Sayre, Paul W. Irving. (2021). Brief, embedded, spontaneous metacognitive talk indicates thinking like a physicist. https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.7590

article_title: Design of the Lifestyle Interventions for severe mentally ill Outpatients in the Netherlands (LION) trial; a cluster randomised controlled study of a multidimensional web tool intervention to improve cardiometabolic health in patients with severe mental illness.
citation: Looijmans A, Jörg F, Bruggeman R, Schoevers R, Corpeleijn E. (2017). Design of the Lifestyle Interventions for severe mentally ill Outpatients in the Netherlands (LION) trial. BMC Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-017-1265-7
title: Traffic Light Method for somatic screening and lifestyle (TLM) web tool
description: The TLM is a web tool originally developed for nurses and patients in one Dutch mental health care organization and advanced by a spin-off company, reviewed by a Delphi expert panel and optimized in a pilot study. It consists of a lifestyle behaviour screening followed by creating a lifestyle plan, and a follow-up phase; it "displays a risk profile with all lifestyle behaviours in green, orange or red, depending on the level of risk". Patients and nurses use it biweekly during regular care visits, and all entered information can be printed as a personal booklet to share with friends and family.
requirements: Used together by patient and nurse during regular care visits, with a follow-up report filled in each biweekly visit for approximately 15 min
constraints: The lifestyle plan part of the tool is only available for participants in the intervention group
target_learners: Community-dwelling patients with severe mental illness and SMI patients living in sheltered facilities
target_learning_goals: Motivation for diet and physical activity behaviour change
examples: In the LION trial, nurses coach patients to assess current lifestyle behaviour with the traffic light method, create a lifestyle plan with maximum three attainable goals, and discuss the plan regularly
key_sources: Looijmans A, Jörg F, Bruggeman R, Schoevers R, Corpeleijn E. (2017). Design of the Lifestyle Interventions for severe mentally ill Outpatients in the Netherlands (LION) trial. BMC Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-017-1265-7

article_title: Improving Primary Healthcare Workflow Using Extreme Summarization of Scientific Literature Based on Generative AI
citation: Gregor Stiglic, Leon Kopitar, Zhe He, Primoz Kocbek, Lucija Gosak, Prithwish Chakraborty, Pablo Meyer, Jiang Bian. (2023). Improving Primary Healthcare Workflow Using Extreme Summarization of Scientific Literature Based on Generative AI. DSHealth at SIGKDD '23, August 6 – 10, 2023, Long Beach, CA. http://www.train4health.eu/
title: TLDR extreme summaries generated with CATTS for rapid literature screening
description: The study used automatically generated extremely short summaries tagged with "TLDR" (short for Too Long, Didn't Read), retrieved from the Semantic Scholar platform alongside full abstracts. These summaries are produced using CATTS (Controlled Abstraction for TLDRs with Title Scaffolding), "a simple yet effective learning strategy for producing TLDRs that utilizes titles as a supplementary training signal". The authors note their previous research found general purpose LLMs such as OpenAI or Pegasus could also perform such extreme summarization with similar performance.
requirements: Abstracts and TLDR summaries retrieved from the Semantic Scholar platform
Questions about abstract content prepared by primary healthcare experts
constraints: TLDRs often consist of only one or two sentences, which the results show can reduce comprehension accuracy
target_learners: health-sciences students with at least basic healthcare knowledge
target_learning_goals: rapid screening of new scientific literature
examples: Each use case study included ten retrieved abstracts, and each participant answered one four-option question per abstract
key_sources: Gregor Stiglic, Leon Kopitar, Zhe He, Primoz Kocbek, Lucija Gosak, Prithwish Chakraborty, Pablo Meyer, Jiang Bian. (2023). Improving Primary Healthcare Workflow Using Extreme Summarization of Scientific Literature Based on Generative AI. DSHealth at SIGKDD '23, August 6 – 10, 2023, Long Beach, CA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15715
